transcript.content: Hi, I'm Dr. Smith. Thanks for coming in. What brings you here today?

I'm here because I've been feeling extremely depressed and down for the past two months. It's been a massive shift from the previous ten months, when I felt unusually energetic and was constantly highly active. I just really need some help figuring out what's going on.
During that ten-month period of high energy and activity, did you experience times when your mood was extremely elevated, irritable, or you felt like you didn’t need much sleep?

Yes, during those months I had times where I felt incredibly happy, euphoric, and full of energy, but I would also get easily irritated and snap over the smallest things. As for the sleep part, I don't really recall having any issues with needing less sleep.
How long did those periods of elevated mood, high energy, and irritability last at a time—were they lasting most of the day, nearly every day for at least one week?
Yes, it lasted much longer than just a week. It was pretty much constant, lasting most of the day, nearly every single day for that entire ten-month stretch.

latest_inference.note: Previously the candidates were ["Bipolar I Disorder", "Bipolar II Disorder"], but based on this conversation, Bipolar II Disorder is no longer a likely candidate because the patient reported a prolonged period of elevated mood and irritability lasting most of the day for nearly ten months, which meets the duration criterion for a manic episode (at least one week). This pattern is consistent with Bipolar I Disorder, which requires at least one full manic episode. Bipolar II Disorder requires only hypomanic episodes (which are less severe and shorter), so it is now ruled out. Therefore, the current candidate is solely Bipolar I Disorder.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient reports a distinct period of abnormally elevated and irritable mood lasting more than one week (in fact, persisting for ten months), along with increased energy and activity, which is characteristic of a manic episode. This is followed by a major depressive episode lasting two months. The presence of a full manic episode supports the diagnosis of Bipolar I Disorder.
